messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 79
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 65

Mr. R is a 79-year-old South Asian man who lives alone in a small apartment near the city’s industrial district. He works three mornings a week at a wholesale warehouse, stacking boxes and checking inventory. He is wiry, quiet, moves with a careful economy—no wasted motion, no sudden turns. When he speaks, his English is precise but halting, as if he is translating from a language he has not used in years. He divorced his wife in the early 1990s and has not remarried. He has two adult children who live in another province; they call once a month, and he keeps the conversations short.

He came to see me after his primary care doctor suggested he “talk to someone” about his sleep problems and his “short temper” with other workers. He agreed reluctantly, but he does not think talking helps.

The story he tells begins in 1971. He was 21, a lance corporal in the infantry. His unit was ambushed in a mangrove swamp near the border. He remembers the heat, the mosquitoes, the way the water came up to his thighs. He remembers the sound of mortars—not the explosions themselves, but the high, thin scream before each impact. During the ambush, he saw his section commander shot in the throat. The man did not fall at once. He tried to speak, but only a red froth came out of the hole. Mr. R carried him for half a mile. The commander died in his arms. Mr. R still feels the weight of that body across his shoulders, the wet warmth, the smell of mud and blood.

After the war, he tried to act normal. He married, had children, worked in a garment factory, then in a warehouse. He never spoke about the ambush or the commander. When his wife asked why he sometimes woke up screaming, he said it was a stomach ache. He avoided loud noises, crowded places, the color red. Eventually his wife stopped asking. She left him, he says, because he was “not there.”

Now, at 79, the war is still in the room with him. He avoids the news, especially anything about the military. He will not attend religious ceremonies where drums are played. At the warehouse, he always puts his back to a wall when he takes a break. He scans every door for exits, every face for potential threats. His co-workers think he is just grumpy and particular. They do not know that the sound of a pallet jack dropping makes him drop to the floor, heart pounding, hands squeezing his old knees.

At night, he lies awake and replays the ambush. Sometimes the commander’s face is replaced by his own son’s. He tells me he is tired—tired of the flashbacks, tired of the constant alertness, tired of feeling like a coward for having survived. He says he has no one to talk to about these things, and even if he did, they would not understand. He recently scored 65 on the PCL-5, which measures severe PTSD symptoms.

He finishes his shifts at the warehouse, goes home, eats a simple dinner of rice and dal, and sits in the dark. He does not watch television. He listens to the hum of the refrigerator and the distant traffic. Sometimes he catches himself crying, but he is not sure why. The feeling that follows is a thick emptiness, as if someone has scraped out the inside of his chest. He does not believe he will ever feel different. He is not even sure he wants to.
